label: Geography
source: Built from the class workbook and homework (Sept–Nov 2026: continents and oceans, the seven natural wonders, the Great Barrier Reef, Antarctica, Easter Island, directions, grid references, scale, contour lines, mental maps). The workbook shows answers but not the questions, so the questions and notes here are ours; diagrams are redrawn.

topics.title: Continents, countries and oceans
topics.summary: The seven continents and the oceans, what a continent, a country and a county are, the Equator and the hemispheres.

images.caption: The seven continents and five oceans. Russia is in both Europe and Asia — the Ural Mountains are the dividing line.

table.title: The seven continents, biggest first
head: Continent
Good to know
rows: Biggest continent, most people (China, India). Mount Everest.
Second biggest. The Equator crosses it. The Sahara Desert, the River Nile, Victoria Falls.
Canada, the USA, Mexico — and Greenland. The Grand Canyon.
Brazil, Argentina, Peru. The Amazon rainforest and the Andes mountains.
Around the South Pole. Coldest, windiest, iciest; no countries, only scientists.
The UK, France, Germany, Italy, Iceland … second smallest.
Also called Australia or Australasia: Australia, New Zealand, Pacific islands. Smallest.

facts: There are **7 continents** (huge areas of land) and **5 oceans** (huge areas of salt water).
On the class map the Atlantic is split into the **North Atlantic** and the **South Atlantic** Ocean, and the Pacific appears on both sides of the map.

**Continent** → **country** → **county**: a continent is a large area of land (and nearby islands) with many countries, e.g. **Europe**. A country is an area of land with its own **government** and people (citizens), e.g. **France**. A county is a **region (part) of a country**, e.g. **Kent**.
Oceans, biggest first: **Pacific**, **Atlantic**, **Indian**, **Southern** (round Antarctica), **Arctic** (round the North Pole).
About **70%** of the Earth's surface is water.
The **Equator** is an imaginary line round the middle of the Earth (0° latitude). It splits the Earth into the **Northern** and **Southern Hemispheres**.
The **Prime Meridian** (0° longitude) runs from pole to pole through **Greenwich, London**. It splits east from west.
**Latitude** lines go across (east–west), like the rungs of a ladder. **Longitude** lines go from the North Pole to the South Pole.
The **UK** is in **Europe**, in the **Northern Hemisphere**, with the **Atlantic Ocean** to its west.

an area of land with its own government and people, e.g. France
a region or part of a country, e.g. Kent or Essex
one of the 5 very large areas of salt water
a smaller area of salt water, often partly surrounded by land (e.g. the North Sea)
imaginary line round the middle of the Earth, 0° latitude
half of the Earth — northern/southern (split by the Equator) or eastern/western
how far north or south of the Equator a place is
how far east or west of the Prime Meridian a place is
the line of 0° longitude, through Greenwich in London

questions.explain: There are seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Oceania.

questions.stem: How many oceans are there?
questions.explain: There are five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.

questions.explain: Asia is the biggest continent, and has the most people. Africa is second.

questions.stem: The UK is in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.stem: About 70% of the Earth's surface is covered by water.
questions.explain: About 71% is water — mostly the oceans. That's why Earth is called the blue planet.

topics.title: The seven natural wonders
topics.summary: The seven natural wonders of the world — what and where they are — and the difference between physical and human (man-made) geography.

images.caption: The seven natural wonders of the world. Can you name the continent each one is in?

table.title: The seven natural wonders
head: Wonder
Where
What makes it a wonder
rows: A huge canyon carved by the Colorado River: about 446 km long and up to 1.8 km deep
The world's biggest coral reef, home to thousands of kinds of sea life
A giant natural bay ringed by granite mountains like Sugarloaf Mountain
The highest mountain on Earth: 8,849 m, in the Himalayas
Glowing green curtains in the sky: particles from the Sun hitting the air
A volcano that grew out of a cornfield in 1943 — people watched it being born
A giant waterfall on the Zambezi — “the smoke that thunders”

facts: The **seven natural wonders of the world**: **Grand Canyon**, **Great Barrier Reef**, **Harbour of Rio de Janeiro**, **Mount Everest**, **Northern Lights**, **Parícutin volcano** and **Victoria Falls**.
They are all made by **nature** — they are **physical** geography. Things built by people are **human** (man-made) geography.
To **describe where a place is**, go from big to small: **continent → country → compass direction / nearby sea or city**.
Then describe its **physical features** (natural: mountains, rivers, climate, plants and animals) and its **human features** (made by people: towns, roads, tourism).
Use precise geography words: not “a big hill” but “a **mountain range**”; not “a big hole” but “a **canyon**”.
keywords: an amazing place made by nature, not by people
the natural world: land, water, weather, volcanoes
people and what they build or do: towns, roads, farming, tourism
a deep valley with steep sides, cut by a river
an opening in the Earth's crust where lava, ash and gas come out
an area of sea partly surrounded by land, where ships shelter
glowing lights in the sky near the poles (the Northern or Southern Lights)

questions.stem: Which natural wonder is labelled {L}?

questions.stem: Which natural wonder is labelled {L}?

questions.stem: Which natural wonder is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: Victoria Falls is in southern Africa, on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe.

questions.stem: Which natural wonder is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: Mount Everest is in the Himalayas in Asia, on the border of Nepal and China.

questions.stem: Which natural wonder is labelled {L}?

questions.stem: Which natural wonder is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The Northern Lights are seen in the far north, near the Arctic — e.g. northern Norway, Iceland, Canada.

questions.stem: I'm a deep, steep-sided canyon in Arizona, USA, carved by the Colorado River. What am I?
questions.explain: The Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon over millions of years. It is about 446 km long and up to about 1.8 km deep.

questions.stem: I'm a giant waterfall on the River Zambezi, between Zambia and Zimbabwe — “the smoke that thunders”. What am I?
questions.explain: Victoria Falls' local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means “the smoke that thunders” — the spray rises like smoke.

questions.stem: I'm the highest mountain on Earth, on the border of Nepal and China. What am I?
questions.explain: Mount Everest is 8,849 m high, in the Himalayas in Asia.

questions.stem: I'm the world's biggest coral reef, off the north-east coast of Australia. What am I?
questions.explain: The Great Barrier Reef is in the Coral Sea, off Queensland, Australia.

questions.stem: I'm a huge natural bay in Brazil, ringed by granite mountains such as Sugarloaf Mountain. What am I?
questions.explain: The harbour (Guanabara Bay) at Rio de Janeiro is one of the biggest natural bays in the world.

questions.stem: I'm a volcano in Mexico that grew out of a farmer's cornfield in 1943. What am I?
questions.explain: Parícutin started as a crack in a cornfield in 1943 and erupted for nine years, growing to over 400 m and burying two villages. Scientists watched a volcano being born.

questions.stem: I'm curtains of green light in the sky near the Arctic, best seen on dark winter nights. What am I?
questions.explain: The Northern Lights (aurora borealis) glow when tiny particles from the Sun hit gases high in the air. Near the South Pole they are the Southern Lights.

questions.stem: How many natural wonders are on the famous list?
questions.explain: The seven natural wonders: Grand Canyon, Great Barrier Reef, Harbour of Rio de Janeiro, Mount Everest, Northern Lights, Parícutin volcano and Victoria Falls.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the seven natural wonders?
questions.explain: The Eiffel Tower is man-made (a human feature). The natural wonders are all made by nature.

questions.stem: Which continent is the Grand Canyon in?
questions.explain: The Grand Canyon is in the USA, in North America.

questions.stem: Which continent is Victoria Falls in?
questions.explain: Victoria Falls is on the River Zambezi in southern Africa.

questions.stem: Which continent is Mount Everest in?
questions.explain: Everest is in the Himalayas, in Asia.

questions.stem: Which country is Parícutin volcano in?
questions.explain: Parícutin is in Mexico (North America).

questions.stem: Which country is the harbour of Rio de Janeiro in?
questions.explain: Rio de Janeiro is a big city on the coast of Brazil, South America.

questions.stem: Which two countries share Victoria Falls?
questions.explain: The River Zambezi forms the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe at the falls.

questions.stem: Mount Everest is in which mountain range?
questions.explain: The Himalayas, in Asia, have all the world's highest mountains.

questions.stem: About how high is Mount Everest?
questions.explain: Everest is 8,849 m. Ben Nevis (the UK's highest) is 1,345 m; Vinson Massif (Antarctica's highest) is 4,892 m.

questions.stem: Which river carved the Grand Canyon?
questions.explain: The Colorado River cut down through the rock over millions of years.

questions.stem: What causes the Northern Lights?
questions.answer: Particles from the Sun hitting gases high in the air
questions.explain: Charged particles from the Sun crash into gases in the atmosphere and make them glow — mostly green.

questions.stem: Physical geography is about the natural world; human geography is about people and what they build.
questions.explain: Physical: mountains, rivers, weather, volcanoes. Human (man-made): towns, roads, farms, tourism.

questions.stem: A physical feature is something made by people.
questions.explain: Physical features are natural (mountains, rivers, waterfalls, reefs). Human (man-made) features are built by people (towns, roads, hotels).

questions.stem: Which of these is a human (man-made) feature?
questions.explain: Human features are made by people — towns, roads, ports, dams. The others are physical (natural) features.

questions.stem: When you describe where a place is, what should you say first?
choices: what you had for lunch there
its grid reference on any map
questions.explain: Start big, then get closer: continent → country → compass direction / near which sea or city. Then describe its physical and human features.

topics.title: The Great Barrier Reef — why is it disappearing?
topics.summary: What the reef is, how coral lives, the threats that are killing it, and what is being done to protect it.

table.title: Why the reef is disappearing
head: Threat
What happens
rows: Coral bleaching: hot water makes coral push out its algae. It turns white and starves; if the heat lasts, it dies.
The sea absorbs carbon dioxide and becomes more acidic, so coral struggles to build its skeleton.
Rain washes soil, fertiliser and pesticide into the sea: cloudy water blocks sunlight and feeds pests.
Outbreaks of these starfish eat huge areas of coral.
Boat anchors, careless divers, overfishing and shipping damage the coral and its food chains.
Plastic and other rubbish in the sea tangles and harms sea life and coral.

facts: The **Great Barrier Reef** is off the **north-east coast of Australia** (Queensland), in the **Coral Sea**, part of the Pacific Ocean.
The nearest big city is **Cairns** in Queensland — the gateway for tourists visiting the reef.
It is the **world's biggest coral reef system**: about **2,300 km** long, made of about **2,900 reefs** and **900 islands**. You can see it from space.
Coral is built by tiny animals called **polyps**. Tiny **algae** live inside them, making food from sunlight and giving coral its colours — so reefs need **warm, clear, shallow, sunny** water.
It is home to thousands of species — over **1,500 kinds of fish**, turtles, sharks, dolphins and dugongs — and it's a **World Heritage Site**.
The biggest threat is **climate change**: warmer seas cause **coral bleaching**. The reef has had several **mass bleaching** events since 2016.
**Bleached ≠ dead**: if the water cools quickly the algae can return. If the heat lasts, the coral dies — and a reef takes many years to recover.

**Protecting it:** marine park zones where fishing is banned, less farm run-off, removing crown-of-thorns starfish, growing and replanting coral — and, most of all, cutting the **greenhouse gases** that warm the planet.
In class you weighed up what damages the reef most (overfishing? tourists?). They all do harm — but scientists agree the **biggest** threat is **climate change** (warming seas → bleaching).
keywords: a ridge in the sea built from the skeletons of coral polyps
the tiny animal that builds coral
tiny living things inside coral that make food from sunlight
coral turning white when the sea is too warm
long-term warming of the Earth, mainly from burning fossil fuels
the sea becoming more acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide
rainwater flowing off the land into rivers and the sea, carrying soil and chemicals
the variety of living things in a place

questions.stem: In which country is the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.explain: It's off the coast of Queensland, Australia.

questions.stem: Off which coast of Australia is the reef?
questions.explain: The reef runs along the north-east coast, in the Coral Sea.

questions.stem: Which sea is the Great Barrier Reef in?
questions.explain: The Coral Sea is part of the Pacific Ocean.

questions.stem: About how long is the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.explain: About 2,300 km — further than from London to Moscow. It's the largest coral reef system in the world.

questions.stem: What are the tiny animals that build coral called?
questions.explain: Coral polyps build hard limestone skeletons; over thousands of years these build up into a reef.

questions.stem: What tiny living things live inside coral, giving it food and its colours?
questions.explain: Algae inside the coral use sunlight to make food (photosynthesis) and share it with the coral.

questions.stem: What is it called when coral turns white because the sea is too warm?
questions.explain: In water that's too warm, coral pushes out its algae, loses its colour and turns white — bleaching.

questions.stem: What causes coral bleaching?
choices: Too much rain on the reef
questions.explain: Rising sea temperatures, caused by climate change, are the main cause of bleaching.

questions.stem: What is the biggest threat to the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.explain: Climate change warms the sea (bleaching) and makes it more acidic. Other threats add to the damage.

questions.stem: Bleached coral is always dead.
questions.explain: Bleached coral is starving but alive. If the water cools quickly the algae can return; if the heat lasts too long, it dies.

questions.stem: Why does the sea become more acidic?
questions.answer: It absorbs carbon dioxide from the air
choices: Rain washes salt out of it
questions.explain: The oceans soak up carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels. More acidic water makes it harder for coral to build its skeleton.

questions.stem: Which animal eats coral and has damaged large parts of the reef?
questions.explain: Outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish eat huge areas of coral. Divers remove them to protect the reef.

questions.stem: How does run-off from farms harm the reef?
questions.answer: Soil and fertiliser wash into the sea, making it cloudy and feeding pests
choices: Farm animals swim out and eat the coral
It makes the sea too cold
questions.explain: Rain washes soil, fertiliser and pesticides off farms in Queensland into rivers and the sea. Cloudy water blocks sunlight, and fertiliser helps crown-of-thorns starfish.

questions.stem: Why do coral reefs need clear, shallow water?
questions.answer: The algae inside the coral need sunlight to make food
choices: So that tourists can see them
questions.explain: Sunlight has to reach the algae for photosynthesis — that's why reefs grow in warm, clear, shallow, sunny seas.

questions.stem: Coral reefs grow best in cold, deep, dark water.
questions.explain: Reef-building coral needs warm, clear, shallow water with plenty of sunlight.

questions.stem: The Great Barrier Reef is so big it can be seen from space.
questions.explain: Yes — it's the biggest structure made by living things on Earth.

questions.stem: Which of these helps to protect the reef?
questions.answer: Banning fishing in some zones of the marine park
choices: Building more ports on the reef
questions.explain: The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park has zones where fishing is banned; there are also rules on farm run-off, starfish culls and coral replanting. Cutting greenhouse gases worldwide helps most of all.

questions.stem: Why does the reef matter to people as well as wildlife?
questions.answer: Tourism brings money and jobs, and the reef protects the coast from waves
choices: It stops it raining in Australia
It makes the sea fresh water
It keeps sharks away from Europe
questions.explain: Millions of visitors bring money and tens of thousands of jobs; the reef also breaks up big waves before they hit the coast.

questions.stem: What does “World Heritage Site” mean?
questions.answer: A place so special that the world agrees to protect it
choices: A place where nobody may visit
A place owned by the United Nations
A place that is always hot
questions.explain: UNESCO lists World Heritage Sites — the Great Barrier Reef has been one since 1981.

questions.stem: Burning coal, oil and gas releases which gas that warms the planet and makes the sea more acidic?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a greenhouse gas: it traps heat (warming the sea) and dissolves in the sea (acidification).

questions.stem: Which Australian city, on the coast of Queensland, is the gateway for visiting the reef?
questions.explain: Cairns is the nearest big city; boats take tourists out to the reef from there.

questions.stem: How do tourists sometimes damage the reef?
questions.answer: Dropping anchors on the coral and breaking bits off as souvenirs
questions.explain: Anchors, careless divers and souvenir collecting break coral. Rules and mooring buoys help to stop this.

questions.stem: How does overfishing harm the reef?
questions.answer: Taking too many fish upsets the food chain that keeps the reef healthy
choices: Fish are needed to make the sea salty
Fishing boats make the water colder
It doesn't harm the reef at all
questions.explain: Some fish eat the seaweed that would smother coral, or eat pests — remove them and the reef suffers.

questions.stem: Coral reefs help to protect the coast from storms.
questions.explain: Reefs break up big waves before they reach the shore, protecting beaches and towns.

topics.source: From the class workbook (22 Sept): “Why is the Great Barrier Reef disappearing?” — where it is (off Cairns), why it matters (jobs, protection from storms) and what damages it (plastic, overfishing, tourists, anchors).

topics.title: Antarctica
topics.source: From the class workbook (30 Sept): the grid map of Antarctica (Snow Hills, Vinson Massif, the South Pole, Mount Erebus) and its physical and human features.
topics.summary: The frozen continent around the South Pole: its mountains and volcano, its wildlife, and its physical and human features.

images.caption: Antarctica, seen from above the South Pole. The places from the class grid map: Vinson Massif, the South Pole, Mount Erebus and Snow Hill(s).

table.title: Places on the class map
head: Place
What it is
rows: The most southerly point on Earth, in the middle of Antarctica. A US research station is there.
An active volcano (3,794 m) with a lava lake, on Ross Island.
Off the Antarctic Peninsula; home to a colony of emperor penguins.
A long mountain range crossing the whole continent.

facts: Antarctica is the **coldest, windiest and driest** continent — about −89 °C has been measured. It counts as a **desert** because so little snow falls.
It is covered by an **ice sheet** up to almost 5 km thick, holding about **70% of the world's fresh water**.
**Physical features**: ice, snow, glaciers, icebergs, mountains (e.g. **Vinson Massif**), volcanoes (e.g. **Mount Erebus**).
**Human features**: research **stations**, **camps** where scientists sleep, runways. Nobody lives there for good.
The **Antarctic Treaty** (1959): Antarctica is for **peace and science** only.
**Roald Amundsen** reached the South Pole first (Dec 1911); Captain **Scott** arrived five weeks later.
Grid maps can use 2-figure coordinates too, e.g. **(07, 43)**: along first, then up.
keywords: a huge, thick layer of ice covering land
a big piece of ice floating in the sea
a base where scientists live and work for a while
the 1959 agreement to use Antarctica only for peace and science

questions.stem: Which place is labelled {L} on the map of Antarctica?
questions.explain: The South Pole is in the middle of Antarctica.

questions.stem: Which place is labelled {L} on the map of Antarctica?
questions.explain: Vinson Massif is in West Antarctica, not far from the base of the Antarctic Peninsula.

questions.stem: Which place is labelled {L} on the map of Antarctica?
questions.explain: Mount Erebus is on Ross Island, by the Ross Sea.

questions.stem: Which place is labelled {L} on the map of Antarctica?
questions.explain: Snow Hill Island is off the Antarctic Peninsula — the long arm pointing towards South America.

questions.stem: Which place is labelled {L} on the map of Antarctica?
questions.explain: The Antarctic Peninsula is the long arm of land reaching towards South America.

questions.stem: Which place is labelled {L} on the map of Antarctica?
questions.explain: The Transantarctic Mountains cross the whole continent, splitting East from West Antarctica.

questions.stem: What is the highest mountain in Antarctica?
questions.explain: Vinson Massif is 4,892 m high.

questions.stem: Which mountain in Antarctica is an active volcano?
questions.explain: Mount Erebus (3,794 m) is the most southerly active volcano on Earth — it even has a lake of lava in its crater.

questions.stem: Which animals breed in a big colony at Snow Hill Island?
questions.explain: Emperor penguins breed on the sea ice there. (Polar bears live in the Arctic, not the Antarctic.)

questions.stem: Antarctica is the … continent on Earth.
questions.explain: The coldest temperature ever measured, about −89 °C, was in Antarctica. It gets so little snow and rain that it counts as a desert.

questions.stem: People live in Antarctica all year round in towns.
questions.explain: Nobody lives there for good. Scientists stay for a while at research stations — about 1,000 in winter and several thousand in summer.

questions.stem: Which of these is a human feature in Antarctica?
questions.explain: Research stations, camps and runways are made by people. Ice, mountains, volcanoes and glaciers are physical features.

questions.stem: Which of these is a physical feature in Antarctica?
questions.explain: Mountains, ice, snow, glaciers and volcanoes are natural — physical features.

questions.stem: About how much of the world's fresh water is frozen in Antarctica's ice?
questions.explain: Antarctica's ice sheet is up to almost 5 km thick and holds most of the world's fresh water.

questions.stem: What does the Antarctic Treaty (1959) say Antarctica may be used for?
questions.explain: Countries agreed to use Antarctica only for peaceful purposes and science.

questions.stem: Who was first to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
questions.explain: Amundsen's Norwegian team got there first; Captain Scott's British team arrived about five weeks later.

questions.stem: Antarctica is bigger than Europe.
questions.explain: Antarctica is about 14 million km² — bigger than Europe and almost twice the size of Australia.

topics.title: Easter Island (Rapa Nui)
topics.source: From the class workbook (6 Oct): Easter Island sketch with labels (Mount Terevaka, Rano Aroi, Ahu Akapu, Hanga Roa, Mataveri, Vaihu, Hotu'iti Bay, Poike). Map redrawn; facts are ours.
topics.summary: A remote Pacific island famous for its giant stone statues — and a sketch map with labels, like the one in class.

images.caption: Easter Island sketch map with labels. North is at the top — so east is on the right.

table.title: Easter Island in brief
rows: South-east Pacific Ocean, about 3,500 km west of Chile
Rapa Nui (also the name of its people and language)
About 900 giant stone statues called moai

facts: Easter Island (**Rapa Nui**) is in the **Pacific Ocean** and belongs to **Chile**. It's one of the most remote places on Earth where people live.
It's a **triangle** of land with an old **volcano** at each corner: **Maunga Terevaka** (north, highest), **Poike** (east) and **Rano Kau** (south-west).
The Rapa Nui people carved about **900 moai** (giant statues) from volcanic rock at the **Rano Raraku** quarry. Many stand on stone platforms called **ahu**, such as **Ahu Akapu**.
**Hanga Roa** is the only town; **Mataveri** is the airport. **Anakena** is the sandy beach in the north.
It's called Easter Island because a Dutch explorer arrived on **Easter Sunday 1722**.
A **sketch map** shows the main features with **labels** and a **north arrow** — check that E is on the right!

a stone platform that moai stand on
a place where stone is dug or cut out

topics.title: Compass directions
topics.summary: The eight points of the compass, opposites, turning, and giving the direction from one place to another on a map.

images.caption: The 8 points of the compass. Clockwise from the top: Never Eat Shredded Wheat.

facts: The four **cardinal points** clockwise from the top: **North, East, South, West** — “**N**ever **E**at **S**hredded **W**heat”.
Halfway between them are **north-east, south-east, south-west, north-west**. North or south always comes first.
On most maps **north is at the top**. On OS maps the grid lines point north.
**“Which direction is B from A?”** — put your finger on **A** (the place after “from”) and look towards **B**.
Opposite directions are a **half turn (180°)** apart. A **quarter turn** is **90°**; one step round the 8-point compass is **45°**.
**Clockwise** goes N → NE → E → SE → S …; **anticlockwise** goes the other way.
The Sun **rises in the east** and **sets in the west**.
A common slip: drawing **E and W the wrong way round** on a sketch map. With north at the top, **east is on the right**.
Answer in a full sentence: “The **bike hire** is **south of** the **hostel**.” The place after “of” is where you start.

topics.title: Grid references and OS maps
topics.summary: Finding places with letter–number squares, 4-figure and 6-figure grid references, and reading OS map symbols and roads.

images.caption: A 4-figure grid reference names a square. Use its bottom-left corner: along the corridor to 25, up the stairs to 43 → 2543.
A 6-figure grid reference pinpoints a spot. Split the square into tenths: 25 and 4 tenths along (254), 43 and 7 tenths up (437) → 254437.

facts: Maps have a **grid** of squares. The lines going up the map are **eastings** — numbered **along the bottom** (and top); they get bigger going east.
The lines going across are **northings** — numbered **up the side**; they get bigger going north.
Always **eastings first**: “**along the corridor, then up the stairs**”.
A **4-figure** grid reference names a **square**: use the numbers of the lines that meet at its **bottom-left corner**.
A **6-figure** grid reference gives an **exact point**: imagine the square cut into **tenths**. The 3rd figure is tenths **along**, the 6th is tenths **up**.
You estimate the tenths by eye — halfway is 5. Being one tenth out is usually fine.
The **key** tells you what the **symbols** mean, e.g. a church, **PH** = pub (public house), **P** = post office, **Sch** = school.
Some maps use **letters and numbers** instead: letters along the bottom, numbers up the side, written **in the middle** of each column and row. Give the **letter first**, e.g. **C4**.
On an **OS map** every grid square is **1 km** across.
Roads: **motorways** are blue (e.g. M25), main **A roads** are green or red (e.g. **A12**), **B roads** are orange/yellow. The number is the road's name.

OS symbols include a church (with a tower or spire, or a plain cross), woods (little trees), a golf course, a hospital, a windmill, a radio mast, a youth hostel and a caravan site — always check the **key**.

topics.title: Scale and distance
topics.source: From the class workbook (Oct): measuring distances on a map (answers in cm and km). Questions are ours.
topics.summary: Using a map's scale to work out real distances — and back again.
facts: The **scale** tells you how much smaller the map is than real life.
Measure **straight-line** distances with a ruler; for **curvy** roads use string or the edge of a sheet of paper.
On OS maps every grid square is **1 km** across — count squares to estimate distances.
keywords: how much smaller the map is than real life
a line marked in km to measure against
the distance as the crow flies

questions.stem: What does the scale of a map tell you?
questions.answer: how much smaller the map is than real life
questions.explain: The scale lets you work out real distances from the map. The key explains symbols; the north arrow shows north.

questions.stem: On a 1:50,000 map, how many centimetres stand for 1 km?
questions.explain: 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm (500 m) in real life — so 2 cm = 1 km.

questions.stem: On a 1:25,000 map, how many centimetres stand for 1 km?
questions.explain: 1 cm = 25,000 cm = 250 m, so 4 cm = 1 km. A 1:25,000 map shows more detail.

questions.stem: How can you measure a curvy road on a map?
questions.answer: lay a piece of string along it, then measure the string
questions.explain: String (or the edge of a sheet of paper, turned at each bend) follows the curves; then measure it against the scale.

questions.stem: What is a “straight-line distance”?
questions.answer: the distance as the crow flies, ignoring bends
choices: the distance to the North Pole
questions.explain: Straight line = as the crow flies. A route along roads or paths is always longer.

questions.stem: Which map shows more detail?
questions.explain: The smaller the second number, the bigger things are drawn — so 1:25,000 shows more detail than 1:50,000.

topics.title: Contour lines and height
topics.source: From the class workbook (20 Oct): “Using contour lines” — heights, and spotting steep land by lots of orange lines. Diagram and questions are ours.
topics.summary: How maps show hills and valleys: contour lines, spot heights, steep and gentle slopes.

images.caption: A hill shown with contour lines every 50 m. The lines are close together on the east side (steep) and far apart on the west (gentle).

table.title: Reading contour lines
head: You see …
It means …
rows: rings getting smaller, numbers going up
a hill; the top is in the middle
a black dot with a number

facts: **Contour lines** join places that are the **same height above sea level**. The number on the line is the height in **metres**.
**Close together = steep. Far apart = gentle. No lines = flat.**
On OS maps contours are **brown/orange**, usually every **10 m** (1:50,000) or **5 m** (1:25,000).
A **spot height** is a black dot with a number: the exact height at that spot.
To find a height between two lines, look at the lines either side: between 100 and 150 m → somewhere in between.
keywords: a line joining places of the same height
a dot with a number giving the exact height
the shape and height of the land
rising quickly — contour lines close together
rising slowly — contour lines far apart

questions.explain: The black dot with 268 next to it is a spot height: the top is 268 m.

questions.answer: between 150 m and 200 m, on a steep slope

questions.explain: C lies between the 150 and 200 lines, where they are close together — steep.

questions.stem: Look at the map of the hill. Point D is …
choices: at the top of the hill
questions.explain: D is outside the lowest (50 m) contour, so it is lower than 50 m.

questions.stem: Look at the map of the hill. Which side is steeper?
questions.explain: On the east side the contour lines are close together — that means steep.

questions.stem: What do contour lines join?
questions.answer: places that are the same height above sea level
questions.explain: Every point on a contour line is the same height; the number tells you the height in metres.

questions.stem: Contour lines close together mean …
questions.explain: Close together = the height changes quickly = steep. (Lots of orange lines = steep!)

questions.stem: Contour lines far apart (or none at all) mean …
questions.explain: Far apart = the height changes slowly = gentle slope. No lines = flat.

questions.stem: What colour are contour lines on OS maps?
questions.explain: Contours are brown or orange. Blue is water; black dots with numbers are spot heights.

questions.stem: What is a spot height?
questions.answer: a dot with a number showing the exact height of that spot
choices: a place where you can see far
questions.explain: Spot heights (a black dot and a number) give the height in metres at one point, often a hilltop.

questions.stem: Which would be the easiest place to walk or build a road?
questions.answer: where there are hardly any contour lines
choices: where the contour lines are bunched together
across the top of a cliff
where the lines form tight circles
questions.explain: Few or no contour lines means flat land — easy for walking, farming and building.

questions.stem: On a 1:50,000 OS map, contour lines are usually drawn every …
questions.explain: The vertical interval is 10 m on 1:50,000 maps (5 m on 1:25,000 maps).

topics.title: Mental maps and sense of place
topics.source: From the class workbook (10 Nov): “Mental mapping & sense of place”.
topics.summary: Maps from memory, and how places make us feel.
facts: A **mental map** is a map drawn **from memory**. It shows the places that matter to you — home, school, a station, a special place.
It's usually **not to scale**, but it should have **labels** and a **key**.
**Sense of place** is the feelings and meanings a place has for you — why you like it, or don't.
Explain with **because**: “I'd like to live near the station **because** I can travel to lots of places quickly.”
keywords: the feelings and meanings a place has for a person

questions.stem: What is a mental map?
questions.answer: a map drawn from memory, showing the places that matter to you
choices: a map printed by Ordnance Survey
questions.explain: A mental map comes from your head. It shows the places you know and use — home, school, a station, your favourite places.

questions.stem: Why do we write “not to scale” on a mental map?
questions.explain: In a mental map, places that matter to you may be drawn big and close; real distances aren't measured.

questions.stem: What is a “sense of place”?
questions.answer: the feelings and meanings a place has for a person
choices: knowing the grid reference of a place
questions.explain: Sense of place is how a place makes you feel and why it matters to you — e.g. a station is special because you can travel anywhere from it.

questions.stem: Two people's mental maps of the same area can look very different.
questions.explain: Everyone uses and feels about places differently, so they remember and draw different things.

questions.stem: What should a good mental map still have, so others can read it?
questions.explain: Labels and a key (symbols for houses, stations, school …) make it readable.
